one_liner: Clustered Erlang/OTP MQTT 3.1/3.1.1/5.0 broker that uses all cores, sustaining loads that saturate single-threaded Mosquitto, at far higher memory and latency.
what_it_does: VerneMQ is a standalone MQTT broker (QoS 0/1/2, MQTT 5 features, shared subscriptions, retained messages, bridges, WebSockets, TLS) that can run as a multi-node cluster with replicated subscription metadata. Clients connect over the standard MQTT wire protocol, so publishers and subscribers written for Mosquitto work unchanged; configuration, authentication (vmq_passwd, vmq_acl, webhooks, Lua/database auth via vmq_diversity) and operations (vmq-admin, HTTP API, Prometheus/Graphite metrics) are VerneMQ-specific.
how_it_is_fast: Each TCP connection (Ranch acceptor) and each subscriber queue (vmq_queue) is its own lightweight Erlang process, so the BEAM schedulers spread work across every core instead of one event loop. Topic matching runs in the publishing session's process against public ETS tables opened with read_concurrency (a topic trie in vmq_reg_trie, with an optional vmq_reg_ordered_trie for sessions holding many subscriptions), and matched messages are pushed straight into each subscriber's queue process. Version 2.2.0 added experimental fan-out sharding (hidden settings fanout.shard_count and fanout.async_handoff) that splits large subscriber lists across worker processes; it postdates the cited benchmark and has no published numbers.
when_to_use: A single Mosquitto instance is pinned at one core and cannot keep up with tens of thousands of QoS 1 messages per second across many independent topics (the cited 50K:50K point-to-point case, where Mosquitto settled at 37.3k/s and VerneMQ held the 50k/s offered load).
You need horizontal scaling or failover: several broker nodes sharing one subscription view, with session takeover between nodes.

Large connection counts (hundreds of thousands to about 1M devices) on a machine with ample RAM, where connection-setup latency matters more than memory (2.47 ms vs 5.74 ms average at 5k connects/s, driven by Mosquitto's p99 tail).
You need offline message storage for persistent sessions plus pluggable auth (webhooks, Redis, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB) inside the broker.
Your team already runs Erlang/OTP and can build and operate an OTP release itself.
when_not_to_use: Latency-sensitive delivery near saturation: in the same vendor test VerneMQ's 50K:50K average pub-to-sub latency was 2,136.62 ms (p99 16.5 s) against 353.82 ms for Mosquitto, and in the low-load basic set Mosquitto had lower average latency in every scenario (for example 0.25 ms vs 0.4 ms point-to-point).
Fan-in through shared subscriptions at high rate: VerneMQ 1.12.6.2 collapsed to 7.6k pub / 3.5k sub per second with about 117 s average latency where Mosquitto delivered 50k in / 40k out.

Memory-constrained hosts or edge gateways: it used about 4x to 22x more memory than Mosquitto in the cited runs (1.2 GB vs 254 MB average at the basic 1K:1K load; 22.4 GB and still rising vs 1 GB at 1M connections; derived from page data) and 90% CPU vs 6% at 50K:50K.
High-rate single-topic fan-out: both VerneMQ and Mosquitto stalled near 80k/s against a 250k/s target, while EMQX and NanoMQ reached it.

You want a vendor-supported binary without paying: official .deb/.rpm packages and Docker images are under the VerneMQ EULA and need a paid subscription for commercial use; the free path is building from source.

integration.form: standalone server (Erlang/OTP release built with `make rel`)
integration.dependencies: Erlang/OTP, libsnappy-dev and a C compiler for the eleveldb NIF (LevelDB offline message store); rebar3-fetched libraries including Ranch, Cowboy, Hackney, Cuttlefish and ReplayQ
integration.platforms: Linux and macOS (CI), ARM builds documented (Raspberry Pi, Apple M1); paid binary packages for Debian/Ubuntu, Amazon Linux 2023 and Alpine on x86-64 and ARM64
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable as a library; it is a network server. Internally one Erlang process per connection and per session queue, with shared state in concurrent ETS tables.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same MQTT 3.1/3.1.1/5.0 wire protocol, so clients need no change, but mosquitto.conf, password/ACL setup, bridges and monitoring must be redone in vernemq.conf and VerneMQ plugins

gotchas: Per-session queues default to max_online_messages = 1000 and max_offline_messages = 1000; excess messages are dropped (queue_message_drop metric) rather than blocking the publisher, so fan-out subscribers that fall more than 1000 messages behind lose data unless you raise the limits. The benchmark post does not say whether these defaults were changed or whether drops occurred.

In a cluster, allow_register_during_netsplit, allow_publish_during_netsplit and allow_subscribe_during_netsplit all default to off, so a netsplit blocks new connections, publishes and subscribes until the cluster is consistent again; allow_anonymous also defaults to off.

Memory growth reports recur: the 2023 benchmark saw memory climb from 18 GB to 22.4 GB after 1M connections were established; issue #2130 (1.12.6.2, memory growing for weeks, closed for inactivity) and open issue #2395 (2.0.1 cluster with reconnecting clients growing to about 16 GB) were never root-caused.

2.2.0 regressed webhook-based auth_on_publish/on_publish latency about 20x (issue #2534, Nagle's algorithm in the Hackney update); 2.2.1 adds connect_options with no_delay to fix it, so skip 2.2.0 if you use webhooks.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick VerneMQ over the catalogued Eclipse Mosquitto when one Mosquitto process is CPU-bound or you need a clustered MQTT broker, and accept far higher memory and worse latency at moderate load; for Kafka-style log streaming or non-MQTT messaging, RabbitMQ or NATS JetStream are the closer fits. No other MQTT broker (EMQX, NanoMQ, HiveMQ) is catalogued yet; in the same vendor test EMQX 4.4.16 and NanoMQ 0.17.0 beat VerneMQ on every enterprise scenario.
verified_claims_summary: EMQ, which sells the competing EMQX broker, ran its Open MQTT Benchmark Suite with XMeter 3.2.4 against VerneMQ 1.12.6.2, Mosquitto 2.0.15 (persistence disabled), EMQX 4.4.16 and NanoMQ 0.17.0, each on one AWS c5.4xlarge (16 vCPU, 32 GB, Ubuntu 22.04.1, CPU model not stated) with 16-byte QoS 1 payloads and no TLS or auth. VerneMQ's only clear wins over Mosquitto are holding the 50k:50k msg/s offered load (Mosquitto plateaued at 37.3k/s using about one core, 6% CPU) and lower average connect latency at 1M connections (2.47 ms vs 5.74 ms, identical p50-p90 of 2 ms); it lost on latency and memory everywhere else and lost to EMQX in every scenario.
status_note: Actively maintained (2.2.1 released in September 2026, commits through October 2026) and Apache-2.0 source you can build and run freely, but official binary packages and Docker images require a paid subscription for commercial use, and the only numeric comparison is a 2023 vendor-run test of version 1.12.6.2.
